newsitem.title: INDIA: Steep Indian farm growth, industry revival seen.
newsitem.headline: Steep Indian farm growth, industry revival seen.

text.p: India's agricultural output is expected to rise steeply in 1996/97 (April-March) while its tardy industrial growth could gather speed in the second half of the year, an independent economic thinktank said on Wednesday.
The Bombay-based Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE) said widespread monsoon rains this year had helped India's agriculture, which in turn could speed up industrial growth.
In its latest review of the Indian economy, the CMIE projected agricultural production to rise by 4.7 percent in 1996/97 from a negative 0.2 percent in the previous year.
"Its (the monsoon's) distribution has been the best in five years," the CMIE said.
India, a predominently agricultural country, depends largely on the four-month June-September monsoon. A good harvest of winter crops normally lifts demand for industrial goods.
The CMIE said India's industrial growth, which started slackening since the second half of 1995/96, was expected to pick up in the second half of the year.

It said three major factors -- high interest rates compounded by a liquidity squeeze, a fall in the growth of rural demand and electricity shortages -- had brought about the decline in industrial production.
According to the CMIE, the situation has now changed. The monsoon has not only helped crops but eased power shortages.
"Thanks to copious rains in 1996, hydro power generation, which had declined by 12.5 percent in 1995/96, is expected to contribute handsomely to power generation in 1996/97," the CMIE said.
Other economists also agreed with the CMIE projections.
"CMIE's forecast is a balanced one... they had been projecting lower growth earlier," said Vasan Sridharan, economic analyst at J.M. Share and Stock Brokers.
"The GDP (gross domestic product) growth is going to be rescued by agriculture this year," he said.
On agriculture, the CMIE has been very optimistic, estimating the 1996/97 foodgrains production higher at 196.3 million tonnes against 185 million in the previous year.
It estimated the 1996/97 kharif or winter foodgrains output at 103.6 million tonnes, up from 97.7 million in the previous year.
"Similarly, production of rabi (summer) foodgrains is also expected to be higher at 92.7 million tonnes during 1996/97 compared to an estimated 87.3 million in 1995/96," it said.
The rains have also boosted the prospects of cash crops.
Oilseeds production in 1996/97 (November-October) is expected to be higher at 23.4 million tonnes compared to 22.6 million in the previous year.
Cotton production in 1996/97 (October-September) is expected to be 16 million bales (one bale is 170 kg), about the same as in the previous year.

India's sugar production in 1996/97 (October-September), however, is expected to fall to around 15 million tonnes from 16.5 million in the previous year, mainly due to a three percent decline in sugarcane output, the CMIE said.
